script.title: Tax extensions for freelancers: how, when, and what they really cost
script.hook: Every spring, a lot of freelancers reach the second week of April and realize their return isn't going to be ready. Maybe a corrected ten ninety-nine hasn't arrived, maybe the expense totals are a mess, or maybe life just got in the way. The answer is usually a tax extension. It's free, it's quick, and it's completely normal. But there's one detail that catches people out every single year, and it can turn a free extension into an expensive one. In this video: what an extension does, how to file one in five minutes, what it costs if you get it wrong, and what to do with the extra six months. Education, not tax advice. Federal rules, twenty twenty-six returns.

segments.heading: Intro
segments.narration: Every spring, a lot of freelancers reach the second week of April and realize their return isn't going to be ready. Maybe a corrected ten ninety-nine hasn't arrived, maybe the expense totals are a mess, or maybe life just got in the way. The answer is usually a tax extension. It's free, it's quick, and it's completely normal. But there's one detail that catches people out every single year, and it can turn a free extension into an expensive one. In this video: what an extension does, how to file one in five minutes, what it costs if you get it wrong, and what to do with the extra six months. Education, not tax advice. Federal rules, twenty twenty-six returns.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. the small paper receipt mascot with a folded corner, round glasses and big eyes holding a calendar with an arrow from April to October. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: What it is
segments.narration: An extension gives you more time to file your return. For a twenty twenty-six return, it moves the filing deadline from Thursday, April fifteenth, twenty twenty-seven to Friday, October fifteenth. It's automatic. You don't need a reason, and the IRS doesn't approve or reject it based on your story. Millions of people file one every year, including plenty of accountants' clients, because preparers spread their work through the summer. Filing an extension doesn't increase your chance of an audit, and it doesn't show up as a mark against you.
segments.on_screen_text: More time to file: Apr 15 → Oct 15
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a calendar page flipping from April to October. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The catch
segments.narration: Here's the detail that matters most. An extension gives you more time to file. It does not give you more time to pay. Any tax you owe for twenty twenty-six is still due on April fifteenth. If you don't pay it, interest starts on April sixteenth, and so does the failure-to-pay penalty of half a percent a month. So the real job in April is not filling in the return. It's estimating what you'll owe, closely enough, and paying that.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a coin still due on the April page. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Estimate
segments.narration: How do you estimate a return you haven't finished? Start with your profit: income from your log minus expenses you know about. Then use a simple rule of thumb from your own numbers. If last year's total tax was about twenty percent of profit, use twenty percent. Subtract the estimated payments you already made for twenty twenty-six. What's left is roughly your balance. Round it up a little. Overpaying is fine, because any extra comes back as a refund or can be applied to twenty twenty-seven.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a simple formula on a card. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Example
segments.narration: Example. Sam, our fictional freelance designer, expects about sixty thousand dollars of profit for twenty twenty-six, and paid nine thousand in estimates. Sam's rate is about twenty percent, so the total tax is roughly twelve thousand. Twelve thousand minus nine thousand is three thousand. Sam rounds up and pays three thousand two hundred with the extension. When Sam files in June, the real balance turns out to be about three thousand and thirty-seven, so about one hundred sixty dollars comes back. No penalty, no interest.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a coin labeled with a small arrow back. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: How one
segments.narration: Now, how to file one. The easiest way: make that payment through IRS Direct Pay, or your IRS online account, and choose extension as the reason. The IRS treats the payment itself as your extension. There's no form to send. Just make sure you pick the right tax year, twenty twenty-six, and save the confirmation. The same works with EFTPS or a debit or credit card payment, as long as you mark it as an extension payment.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a laptop with a payment screen. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: How two
segments.narration: The second way is Form forty-eight sixty-eight. It's one page: your name, address, Social Security number, your estimate of total tax, what you've paid, and the balance. You can e-file it free through IRS Free File, whatever your income, or through most tax software. If you can't pay anything right now, this is the way to go: file the form anyway, so at least you avoid the much bigger failure-to-file penalty.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a single-page form with a stamp. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Penalties
segments.narration: Let's put real numbers on getting it wrong. Say you owe three thousand dollars and do nothing at all until October. Failure to file is five percent a month, up to twenty-five percent. Failure to pay is half a percent a month. In a month when both apply, the filing penalty is reduced by the paying one, so the combined charge is five percent. Six months late, unextended and unpaid, costs about seven hundred and sixty dollars in penalties, plus interest. With an extension and a payment, it can cost nothing.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a tall stack next to an empty space. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Partial
segments.narration: What if you can only pay part of it? Pay what you can, and file the extension anyway. The failure-to-pay penalty and interest only apply to the unpaid part. Then, when you file, if you still owe, you can set up a payment plan online. While you're on a plan, after filing on time, the failure-to-pay penalty drops to a quarter of a percent a month. Interest still applies, so pay it down as fast as you can.
segments.on_screen_text: Can't pay it all? Pay some, still extend
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a coin split into pieces. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Q1
segments.narration: Here's the second thing people forget. April fifteenth is also the due date for your first estimated payment for twenty twenty-seven. The extension doesn't touch it. So on April fifteenth an extension filer usually makes two payments: the estimated twenty twenty-six balance, marked as an extension, and the twenty twenty-seven first-quarter estimate, marked as estimated tax, form ten forty E S, tax year twenty twenty-seven. Two payments, two tax years.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. two coins with different labels. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: States
segments.narration: Your state may work differently. Many states accept the federal extension automatically. Some want their own form or payment. And just like the IRS, almost none of them give you more time to pay. Check your state tax agency's website for its extension rule, and make a state payment on April fifteenth if you expect to owe.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a map pin with a small calendar. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Upsides
segments.narration: Extensions have a couple of real upsides for freelancers. If you want to put money in a SEP IRA for twenty twenty-six, you can do it up until the extended deadline. That's up to six extra months to save, and the deduction still counts for twenty twenty-six. And you get time to get your records right: a missed deduction you find in July saves more than the extension ever costs. One limit: IRA and HSA contributions for twenty twenty-six still have to be made by April fifteenth, extension or not.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a small vault with an October tag. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Six months
segments.narration: Now the trap. Six months feels like forever, and then it's October and the return still isn't done. So pick a finish date in May or June and book it like a client meeting. Interest keeps running on anything you didn't pay, so finishing earlier tells you the real number sooner. And remember, your June fifteenth and September fifteenth estimates are due on time while you're still on the extension.
segments.on_screen_text: Pick a finish date in May or June
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a calendar block labeled 'finish return'. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Mistakes
segments.narration: Three mistakes to avoid. One: paying the extension estimate as an estimated tax payment for twenty twenty-seven, so it lands in the wrong year. Choose extension, tax year twenty twenty-six. Two: thinking the extension covers your state. Check. Three: forgetting to file in October because nothing reminds you. Put October first in your calendar with the words finish the return, and October fifteenth with the words last day.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. three small warning signs. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Records
segments.narration: One practical tip for extension season. Make a single folder, paper or digital, called twenty twenty-six return, and put everything in it as it arrives: each ten ninety-nine, the corrected forms, your expense totals, your mileage total, home office measurements and the extension payment confirmation. When you sit down in May or June, you're not hunting for anything. Most extensions that run late do so because the paperwork is scattered, not because the return is hard.

segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a folder filling with labeled papers. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Recap
segments.narration: Recap. An extension is free, automatic and normal. It moves filing to October fifteenth, not paying. Estimate your balance from profit times your own rate, minus payments, round up, and pay it by April fifteenth, choosing extension as the reason. Or file Form forty-eight sixty-eight. Pay the first twenty twenty-seven estimate on the same day. Then pick a finish date and keep the June and September payments on time. In this video we'll go through how it works, why it's often better than quarterly payments, and worked examples for a side gig and for a couple where one person freelances. Education, not tax advice. Federal rules, twenty twenty-six figures.
segments.on_screen_text: Skip quarterly payments (if you have a paycheck)
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. the small paper receipt mascot with a folded corner, round glasses and big eyes holding a pay stub and a laptop. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Who
segments.narration: This works if you have wages from an employer, or you file jointly with someone who does. It doesn't work if freelancing is your only income. In that case, quarterly payments are still the tool. But a lot of people freelance alongside a job, or are the freelancing half of a two-income household. For them, withholding is usually the simplest way to stay on top of the tax.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. two figures, one with a briefcase. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The rule
segments.narration: The rule that makes it work: for the underpayment penalty, the IRS treats tax withheld from wages as if it were paid evenly through the year, on each quarterly due date, no matter when it was actually withheld. Estimated payments count on the day you make them. So with withholding, it doesn't matter if you only increase it in October. It still counts as paid on time in April, June and September. That makes withholding much more forgiving than quarterly payments.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a row of evenly spaced coins on a calendar. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: How
segments.narration: How to do it. Give your employer a new Form W-4. On line four C, extra withholding, write the extra amount you want taken from each paycheck. That's it. Most payroll systems let you update it online, and it starts on the next paycheck or two. You can change it as often as you like, so you can raise it after a big freelance project and lower it again later.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a form with one line highlighted. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: How much
segments.narration: How much extra? You need two numbers: how much tax the freelance income adds, and how many paychecks are left in the year. The tax it adds is more than you might think, because there are two parts. Self-employment tax of about fifteen point three percent on most of your freelance profit, plus income tax at your top bracket rate. The IRS Tax Withholding Estimator on irs dot gov will work it out if you enter your freelance income as self-employment income.
segments.on_screen_text: Extra tax = SE tax + income tax at your bracket
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. two small stacks added together. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Side gig
segments.narration: Example one: Jordan, single, earns sixty thousand dollars in salary and makes about eight thousand dollars of profit from weekend photography. Self-employment tax on eight thousand is about one thousand one hundred and thirty dollars. The photography profit, after the deductions that come with it, is taxed at Jordan's twelve percent bracket, adding roughly seven hundred dollars of income tax. So the gig adds about eighteen hundred dollars of tax. Paid every two weeks, with twenty-six paychecks, that's about seventy dollars extra per check.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a pay stub with a small coin. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Couple
segments.narration: Example two: a married couple filing jointly. Alex earns seventy thousand dollars in salary. Riley freelances, with forty thousand dollars of profit. Self-employment tax is only on Riley's profit: about five thousand six hundred and fifty dollars. Income tax is on their combined income. With the twenty twenty-six joint standard deduction of thirty-two thousand two hundred dollars and the qualified business income deduction, their income tax comes to about seven thousand six hundred dollars.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. two figures with coin stacks. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Couple two
segments.narration: Without Riley's freelance income, their tax would have been about four thousand and forty dollars, and Alex's withholding covers that. So freelancing adds about nine thousand two hundred and twenty dollars. That's about twenty-three percent of Riley's profit, because the freelance income stacks on top of Alex's salary. Covering it with Alex's withholding means about three hundred and fifty-five dollars extra per biweekly paycheck. Or quarterly payments of about two thousand three hundred and five dollars. Or a mix.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a pay stub with an arrow. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Why better
segments.narration: Why is withholding often better? First, no deadlines to miss. Second, it's spread out in small amounts, which is easier on cash flow than four big payments. Third, the even-payment rule means a late-year fix still counts. And fourth, there's no new account or payment system to set up. The trade-off is that the money leaves the paycheck before you see it, so if freelance income is very unpredictable, you might over or under withhold.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a checklist with four ticks. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Mix
segments.narration: Many people use a mix. Withholding covers a steady base amount, the tax on the freelance income you're confident about. Then, if a big project lands, you make a one-off estimated payment for that quarter, or raise the withholding for the rest of the year. This gives you the predictability of withholding and the flexibility of estimates.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a big coin and a row of small coins. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Safe harbor
segments.narration: Whichever you choose, the penalty test is the same. You're generally safe if withholding plus estimated payments cover at least one hundred percent of last year's total tax, or one hundred and ten percent if last year's adjusted gross income was over one hundred fifty thousand dollars. Or ninety percent of this year's tax. For a couple, last year's numbers are on last year's joint return.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a shield with three numbers. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Self-em
segments.narration: What about the freelancer's own records? Even when the spouse's withholding pays the tax, the freelancer still files Schedule C and Schedule SE, keeps an income and expense log, and tracks deductions. The withholding only changes how the tax is paid, not what's owed. And it's worth agreeing, as a couple, how the freelance income and the extra withholding are shared, so nobody feels their paycheck is covering someone else's business.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. two forms on a desk. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Changes
segments.narration: Recheck at least twice a year: once after you file, using the real numbers from your return, and once in the fall, when you know how the year is going. If the freelance work has grown, raise the amount. If it's shrunk, lower it. A five-minute W-4 change in September is much easier than a surprise in April.
segments.on_screen_text: Recheck after filing and in the fall
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a dial being turned on a calendar. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: States
segments.narration: Your state income tax works the same way. Most states have their own withholding form, or use the federal W-4. Extra state withholding can cover the state tax on your freelance income, so you can skip state estimated payments too. Check your state's rule for how it treats withholding for its penalty.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a map pin with a pay stub. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Mid-year
segments.narration: What if you're reading this mid-year and haven't paid anything on your freelance income yet? Withholding can still fix it. Because withholding counts as paid evenly, adding the whole year's extra tax over your remaining paychecks covers the earlier quarters too. Say Jordan starts in July with thirteen paychecks left: eighteen hundred divided by thirteen is about one hundred and forty dollars a check. It's a bigger bite, but it can wipe out a penalty that quarterly payments couldn't.
segments.on_screen_text: Late start? Spread it over what's left
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a calendar with coins on the later months. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Two jobs
segments.narration: And if you have more than one job, or both spouses work and one also freelances, the W-4 has a step for multiple jobs. Use the IRS estimator rather than the paper worksheet, because it handles all the incomes at once and tells you which W-4 to change and by how much. Put the extra on the highest-paying job's W-4, so it's withheld from the biggest paycheck and is easiest to keep up.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. two pay stubs with one highlighted. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Recap
segments.narration: Recap. If you or your spouse has a paycheck, you can cover freelance tax with extra withholding on line four C of the W-4. Withholding counts as paid evenly through the year, so it's forgiving. Work out the extra tax, self-employment tax plus income tax at your bracket, and divide by the paychecks left. Use a mix for lumpy income, recheck twice a year, and keep filing Schedule C and SE as normal. The free calculator in the description helps you size the extra tax. script.title: What your 2026 tax return says about your freelance business
script.hook: Most people file their tax return and never look at it again. But for a freelancer, your return is the most honest report on your business you'll get all year. It tells you what you really earned, what you really kept, what your time was worth, and how much to save for next year. In this video, we'll read a twenty twenty-six return like a business report, one number at a time, and turn each one into a decision for twenty twenty-seven. You'll need your return open, or the summary from your software. Education, not tax advice.

segments.heading: Intro
segments.narration: Most people file their tax return and never look at it again. But for a freelancer, your return is the most honest report on your business you'll get all year. It tells you what you really earned, what you really kept, what your time was worth, and how much to save for next year. In this video, we'll read a twenty twenty-six return like a business report, one number at a time, and turn each one into a decision for twenty twenty-seven. You'll need your return open, or the summary from your software. Education, not tax advice.
segments.on_screen_text: Your tax return = your business report
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. the small paper receipt mascot with a folded corner, round glasses and big eyes reading a report with glasses on. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Example
segments.narration: We'll use Sam again, our fictional freelance designer and single filer. Sam's clients paid sixty-eight thousand five hundred dollars in twenty twenty-six. Expenses were eight thousand five hundred, so profit was sixty thousand. Total federal tax was about twelve thousand and thirty-seven dollars. Sam worked about one thousand four hundred billable hours and another four hundred on admin, sales and learning. Write down your own versions of these numbers as we go.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a profile card with coins. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Number one
segments.narration: Number one: gross receipts, line one of Schedule C. That's your revenue. Compare it with last year. Did it grow? By how much? And where did it come from: more clients, higher rates, or more hours? Revenue that grew because you worked more hours is fragile. Revenue that grew because your rates went up is much healthier, because it doesn't cost you more of your life.
segments.on_screen_text: 1. Revenue: where did growth come from?
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a bar chart with labels. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Number two
segments.narration: Number two: total expenses, and your expense ratio. Divide expenses by revenue. Sam's is eight thousand five hundred divided by sixty-eight thousand five hundred: about twelve percent. For many service freelancers, ten to twenty percent is normal. Much higher, and it's worth looking at subscriptions and tools you no longer use. Much lower, and you may be missing deductions, or under-investing in your business.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a pie with a small slice. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Number three
segments.narration: Number three: net profit, line thirty-one of Schedule C. This is the number everything else is built on: your self-employment tax, your income tax, your retirement contribution limits, even your health insurance subsidy. Divide it by revenue for your profit margin. Sam's is about eighty-eight percent. Then divide profit by twelve. That's your average monthly profit. Sam's is five thousand dollars a month, before tax.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a coin stack with a monthly divider. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Number four
segments.narration: Number four: your total tax, on the total tax line of Form ten forty. Divide it by profit. That's your real federal rate. Sam's is twelve thousand and thirty-seven divided by sixty thousand: about twenty percent. Most freelancers are surprised it's that high, because of the fifteen point three percent self-employment tax. Add your state rate, and that's the starting point for your twenty twenty-seven set-aside percentage.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a fraction on a card. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Number five
segments.narration: Number five: your take-home. Profit minus total tax, minus state tax. For Sam, sixty thousand minus about twelve thousand federal is forty-eight thousand, before state. That's four thousand a month. This is your real salary. Compare it with what you'd earn in a job doing the same work, and remember a job would add health insurance, paid time off and a retirement match. If the gap is big, it's a pricing problem, not a tax problem.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a wallet with coins. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Number six
segments.narration: Number six: your real hourly rate. Take-home divided by all the hours you worked, billable and not. Sam's forty-eight thousand divided by one thousand eight hundred hours is about twenty-six dollars and seventy cents an hour. If Sam bills seventy-five dollars an hour, that's a shock. But it's the true number. To raise it, you can raise rates, cut non-billable hours, or both. Track it every year.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a clock with a small coin. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Number seven
segments.narration: Number seven: adjusted gross income. For Sam it's fifty-five thousand seven hundred and sixty-one dollars. This one decides your twenty twenty-seven safe harbor: if it's over one hundred fifty thousand dollars, the safe harbor is one hundred and ten percent of this year's tax instead of one hundred percent. It also affects marketplace health insurance subsidies, IRA deduction limits and student loan payments. Write it down.
segments.on_screen_text: 7. AGI decides next year's safe harbor
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a sticky note with one number. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Number eight
segments.narration: Number eight: estimated payments made, and the balance or refund. Sam paid nine thousand and owed about three thousand and thirty-seven more. A balance of a few hundred dollars means your set-aside is about right. A balance in the thousands means you need a higher percentage, or you stopped setting aside when money got tight. A big refund means you lent the IRS money interest-free all year. Either way, adjust now, not next April.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a coin with a small arrow. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Number nine
segments.narration: Number nine: the deductions you claimed. Look at each category: home office, car, software, equipment, phone, health insurance, retirement. Is anything missing that you know you paid for? Did you take the home office deduction? Did you track mileage? Every missed deduction at Sam's income costs about twenty-three cents per dollar, counting both income tax and self-employment tax. Set up a way to track it from May.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a receipt with a star. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Number ten
segments.narration: Number ten: retirement contributions, or the lack of them. If there's nothing on the line for SEP, solo four-oh-one-k or IRA contributions, that's a decision to make this year. At Sam's income, a SEP contribution of about eleven thousand dollars would have cut about one thousand and seventy dollars of federal income tax and built savings at the same time. You don't need to decide the amount now, just the account.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a small jar with a lid. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Decisions
segments.narration: Now turn the numbers into decisions. From number four: your set-aside percentage for twenty twenty-seven. From number six: whether to raise your rates. From numbers seven and eight: your safe harbor amount and your next quarterly payment. From nine: what to start tracking. From ten: which retirement account to open. Five decisions, and each one makes next year's return better.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a list with five checkboxes. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Folder
segments.narration: Last, the boring part that saves you later. Save a PDF of the full return, federal and state, in a folder with the year on it, along with the ten ninety-nines, your income and expense logs, mileage log and payment confirmations. Keep it at least three years, and longer for records of equipment or property you still own. And copy your ten numbers onto one page you'll see again next April, so you can compare.
segments.on_screen_text: Save the return + a one-page summary
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a folder with a sticky note. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Clients
segments.narration: There's one more number your return doesn't show, but your records do: how much of your revenue came from your biggest client. Add up each client's payments for twenty twenty-six. If one client was more than about forty percent of your income, that's a risk worth planning for. It doesn't mean dropping them. It means building a cash cushion, keeping your pipeline full, and making sure your rate with them still makes sense.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a pie with one large slice. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Health
segments.narration: And look at what you paid for health insurance. If you bought a marketplace plan, Form eighty-nine sixty-two on your return compares the subsidy you got during the year with the one you qualified for. A big repayment means your income estimate on the marketplace was too low. Update it now for twenty twenty-seven. If you deducted self-employed health insurance, check the amount is on Schedule one; it's one of the easier deductions to miss.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a heart next to a small form. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Compare
segments.narration: If you have last year's return too, put the two side by side and compare all ten numbers. The direction matters more than the level. Rising revenue with a falling hourly rate means you're working more for less. A rising expense ratio might be fine if it bought you new clients. A shrinking balance due means your set-aside habit is working. Two years of numbers tell you more than either one alone.

segments.heading: Step one
segments.narration: Step one: profit so far. Add up what clients actually paid you from January through April, and subtract your business expenses for the same months. If you keep a simple income and expense log, this takes five minutes. If you don't, your business bank account statement is a good enough start. Write down the number. Let's say Maya, a fictional freelance writer, made twenty-four thousand dollars of profit in the first four months.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a short bar chart with four bars. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Step two
segments.narration: Step two: project the full year. The simple version is to multiply by three, because four months is a third of the year. For Maya, that's seventy-two thousand dollars. Then adjust for what you know. Is a big client contract ending in the summer? Is December always slow? Do you have a large project booked for the fall? Maya knows one client is pausing in July, so she adjusts down to about sixty thousand.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a longer bar chart with one bar shaded. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Step three
segments.narration: Step three: estimate the federal tax. If you have last year's return, use your own real rate: total tax divided by profit. If not, here are rough rates from twenty twenty-six for a single filer with the standard deduction. At thirty thousand dollars of profit, about seventeen percent. At sixty thousand, about twenty percent. At one hundred twenty thousand, about twenty-four percent. Maya's sixty thousand projection means about twelve thousand dollars of federal tax.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. three coin stacks of different heights. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Step four
segments.narration: Step four: compare with your safe harbor. Your safe harbor is last year's total tax, or one hundred and ten percent of it if last year's adjusted gross income was over one hundred fifty thousand. Say Maya's twenty twenty-six tax was nine thousand dollars. Her safe harbor is two thousand two hundred and fifty a quarter. But her projected twenty twenty-seven tax is twelve thousand. So there are three possible situations, and each one has a different move.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. two coins side by side. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Case one
segments.narration: Case one: your projected tax is higher than the safe harbor, like Maya. Keep paying the safe harbor amount each quarter. That protects you from the underpayment penalty. But the gap, three thousand dollars for Maya, will be due next April. So save it in your tax account as you go. About seven hundred and fifty dollars a quarter, on top of her estimates. Don't spend it just because the IRS isn't asking for it yet.
segments.on_screen_text: Case 1: higher → pay safe harbor, save the gap
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a jar with two lines on it. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Case two
segments.narration: Case two: your projected tax is much lower than last year, because income dropped. Then you may be able to pay ninety percent of this year's tax instead. Example: last year's tax was twelve thousand and thirty-seven, on sixty thousand of profit. This year you expect forty thousand of profit and about seven thousand four hundred and twenty-seven of tax. Ninety percent is about six thousand six hundred and eighty-four, roughly one thousand six hundred and seventy-one a quarter instead of three thousand and ten.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a smaller coin next to a bigger one. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Case two b
segments.narration: The catch with the ninety percent method: it's based on a projection, and if your income recovers in the fall, your earlier payments may turn out too small. Each quarter is tested separately, so a big fourth quarter doesn't fix the first three. If your income comes in late in the year, the annualized income method, on Schedule A I of Form twenty-two ten, can match your payments to when you actually earned the money. Software handles it, but you need monthly records.
segments.on_screen_text: If income recovers: the annualized method
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a calendar with a jagged line. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Case three
segments.narration: Case three: projected tax is close to the safe harbor. Then keep doing what you're doing. Pay the safe harbor amount, keep setting aside your percentage, and recheck in August. Most freelancers will be in this case most years, and that's exactly the point of the safe harbor: it lets you stop worrying about the exact number.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a steady line on a chart. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Retirement
segments.narration: Now the money-saving part. If your projection is solid, decide your retirement account now. At sixty thousand of profit, a SEP IRA allows about eleven thousand dollars, and a solo four-oh-one-k allows more, because you can add an employee deferral on top. Spreading contributions monthly from May is easier than finding the money in December. And every contribution to a traditional SEP or solo four-oh-one-k lowers this year's income tax, so you can lower your set-aside a little to match.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a small jar with coins dropping in. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Rates
segments.narration: Next, rates. If your projection shows a lower year than you want, the fastest fix is usually pricing, not tax. A five percent rate increase for new projects from May adds more take-home than most deductions. If you haven't raised rates in a year, mid-year is a good time to do it for new clients, and January for existing ones.
segments.on_screen_text: If the year looks thin: raise rates
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a price tag with a small arrow up. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Expenses
segments.narration: And expenses. Mid-year is the time to buy what you actually need for your work: a computer that's slowing you down, software that saves you hours, a course that lets you charge more. Equipment can usually be deducted in the year you buy it. But don't buy things just for the deduction. A thousand-dollar expense saves around two hundred and thirty dollars at Sam's income. You're still nearly eight hundred dollars down.
segments.on_screen_text: Buy what you need, not for the write-off
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a laptop with a small tag. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Repeat
segments.narration: Finally, put two more check-ins in your calendar: late August, before the September payment, and early December, before the year ends. Same four steps, ten minutes each once you've done it once. Each time, update the projection, check which case you're in, and adjust your next payment or your set-aside.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a calendar with three marks. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: State
segments.narration: Do the same projection for your state. Most states with an income tax use the federal profit as the starting point, so you already have the hard part. Multiply your projected profit by your state's rough rate, compare it with what you're paying, and adjust. If you're in a state with a different schedule, like California's forty percent payment in June, the mid-year check is even more important, because June is the biggest state payment of the year.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a map pin next to a telescope. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Health
segments.narration: And update your health insurance estimate. If you're on a marketplace plan with a subsidy, the subsidy is based on the income you projected when you signed up. If your mid-year projection is much higher, update your application now, so you don't have to repay a big amount when you file. If it's much lower, you may qualify for more help starting next month. It takes ten minutes on the marketplace site.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a heart with a small dial. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Recap
segments.narration: Recap. Add up profit for January to April. Project the year and adjust for what you know. Estimate the tax with your real rate. Compare with your safe harbor. Higher: pay the safe harbor and save the gap. Lower: consider the ninety percent method or the annualized method. Close: carry on. Then pick a retirement account, review your rates, and buy what you need. The Quarterly Tax Tracker in the description does the projection for you from your logs. script.title: The June 15 payment, worked out for three freelancers
script.hook: Six weeks from now, on Tuesday, June fifteenth, twenty twenty-seven, the second estimated tax payment of the year is due. It catches a lot of people out, because it comes just two months after April. In this video, we'll work out the June payment for three fictional freelancers: one earning about thirty thousand dollars of profit, one about sixty thousand, and one about one hundred twenty thousand. Then we'll cover what changes if your income has dropped, if you overpaid in April, or if you applied a refund. Education, not tax advice. Federal rules, twenty twenty-six figures for last year's tax.

segments.heading: Intro
segments.narration: Six weeks from now, on Tuesday, June fifteenth, twenty twenty-seven, the second estimated tax payment of the year is due. It catches a lot of people out, because it comes just two months after April. In this video, we'll work out the June payment for three fictional freelancers: one earning about thirty thousand dollars of profit, one about sixty thousand, and one about one hundred twenty thousand. Then we'll cover what changes if your income has dropped, if you overpaid in April, or if you applied a refund. Education, not tax advice. Federal rules, twenty twenty-six figures for last year's tax.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. the small paper receipt mascot with a folded corner, round glasses and big eyes holding three small cards. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Calendar
segments.narration: First, why June comes so fast. The IRS splits the year into four payment periods, but they're not equal. January through March is paid in April. April and May, just two months, are paid in June. June, July and August are paid in September. And September through December is paid the following January. So June's payment covers the shortest period, but if you use the safe harbor, it's the same amount as all the others.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. four blocks of different widths. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Safe harbor
segments.narration: Quick reminder of the safe harbor. You generally avoid the underpayment penalty if each payment is at least a quarter of last year's total tax, or a quarter of one hundred and ten percent of it if last year's adjusted gross income was over one hundred fifty thousand dollars. Last year here means twenty twenty-six, the return you just filed. The other option is ninety percent of this year's tax, which we'll come to.
segments.on_screen_text: Safe harbor: ¼ of 2026 total tax
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a shield with a fraction. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Ana
segments.narration: Freelancer one: Ana, a part-time illustrator and single filer. Her twenty twenty-six profit was thirty thousand dollars. Her self-employment tax was about four thousand two hundred and thirty-nine dollars, and income tax about nine hundred and forty-two, so total tax was about five thousand one hundred and eighty-one. Her adjusted gross income was well under one hundred fifty thousand, so the safe harbor is one hundred percent.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a profile card with a paintbrush. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Ana pay
segments.narration: A quarter of five thousand one hundred and eighty-one is one thousand two hundred and ninety-five dollars and twenty-five cents. Ana rounds up to one thousand two hundred and ninety-six. She paid that in April, and pays the same on June fifteenth. To be ready, she needs to set aside about six hundred and fifty dollars a month from April and May. Her income is lumpy, so she moves a fixed percentage of each payment into her tax account, rather than a fixed amount.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a coin labeled with a small tag. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Sam
segments.narration: Freelancer two: Sam, the designer we've followed all year. Twenty twenty-six profit, sixty thousand dollars. Self-employment tax about eight thousand four hundred and seventy-eight, income tax about three thousand five hundred and fifty-nine, total about twelve thousand and thirty-seven. Adjusted gross income fifty-five thousand seven hundred and sixty-one. So Sam's safe harbor is a quarter of twelve thousand and thirty-seven: about three thousand and ten dollars a payment.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a profile card with a pencil. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Sam pay
segments.narration: Sam paid three thousand and ten on April fifteenth, and pays the same on June fifteenth. That's about one thousand five hundred dollars a month to set aside for April and May. Sam's projection for twenty twenty-seven is a bit higher than last year, about sixty-six thousand, so Sam keeps paying the safe harbor but also saves an extra hundred dollars a month for next April's balance.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a jar with two lines. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Jo
segments.narration: Freelancer three: Jo, a software consultant. Twenty twenty-six profit, one hundred twenty thousand dollars. Self-employment tax about sixteen thousand nine hundred and fifty-five, income tax about eleven thousand five hundred and six, total about twenty-eight thousand four hundred and sixty-two. Jo's adjusted gross income was about one hundred eleven thousand five hundred, under one hundred fifty thousand. So Jo's safe harbor is still one hundred percent.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a profile card with a laptop. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Jo pay
segments.narration: A quarter of twenty-eight thousand four hundred and sixty-two is seven thousand one hundred and fifteen dollars and fifty cents. Jo pays seven thousand one hundred and sixteen. If Jo's adjusted gross income had been over one hundred fifty thousand, the safe harbor would be one hundred and ten percent: about seven thousand eight hundred and twenty-seven a payment. That's why it's worth knowing which side of the line you're on.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. two coins, one slightly larger. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Dropped
segments.narration: Now, what if your income dropped? Say Sam loses a big client and now expects forty thousand dollars of profit in twenty twenty-seven, with about seven thousand four hundred and twenty-seven of tax. Ninety percent of that is about six thousand six hundred and eighty-four. Under the ninety percent method, each payment is twenty-two and a half percent of this year's tax, and the test is cumulative. By June fifteenth, Sam needs forty-five percent in total: about three thousand three hundred and forty-two.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a bar chart dropping. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Dropped two
segments.narration: Sam already paid three thousand and ten in April. Three thousand three hundred and forty-two minus three thousand and ten leaves only about three hundred and thirty-two dollars due in June. That's a big cash-flow difference. But remember the risk: if Sam's income recovers in the fall, the June payment may turn out too small. Keep records, and recheck before September.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. two coins adding up. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Overpaid
segments.narration: What if you overpaid in April, or applied your twenty twenty-six refund to twenty twenty-seven? Applied refunds count as paid on April fifteenth. So if Sam had a one thousand dollar refund applied, plus a three thousand and ten payment, Sam has four thousand and ten credited, and only needs about two thousand and ten more by June fifteenth to stay on the safe harbor schedule. Check your IRS online account to see exactly what's been credited to twenty twenty-seven.
segments.on_screen_text: Credits count: check your online account
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a laptop showing a balance. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: How to pay
segments.narration: Paying is the same as April. IRS Direct Pay or your online account: estimated tax, form ten forty E S, tax year twenty twenty-seven. Or EFTPS, scheduled by eight p.m. Eastern the day before. You can schedule the payment today, dated June fifteenth, and not think about it again. Save the confirmation in your tax folder.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a calendar with a coin. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: States
segments.narration: Don't forget your state. Many states also have a June fifteenth payment, but the amount isn't always a quarter. California, for example, wants forty percent of its yearly estimate in June, and nothing in September. Check your state tax agency's site for its schedule, and schedule that payment at the same time.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a map pin with a coin. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Higher
segments.narration: What if your income is well above last year's? Take Jo, who expects one hundred fifty thousand dollars of profit this year instead of one hundred twenty. The safe harbor still protects Jo from the penalty as long as each payment is seven thousand one hundred and sixteen. But Jo's twenty twenty-seven tax will be closer to thirty-seven thousand, so about nine thousand will be due next April. Jo keeps paying the safe harbor and saves the difference each month.
segments.on_screen_text: Income up? Safe harbor + save the gap
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a jar with two marked levels. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Missed
segments.narration: And if you miss June fifteenth? Pay as soon as you can. The underpayment penalty works like interest, figured on the amount that was late and for how many days. A payment a week late costs very little. A payment skipped until next April costs months of it. So never skip a payment because you can't make it on the day. Pay late, pay part, or pay what you can, and catch up by September. Then set a reminder a week before the next one, so it doesn't happen twice.
segments.on_screen_text: Missed it? Pay late, not never
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a coin rolling in just after a line. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Recap
segments.narration: Recap. June fifteenth covers April and May, but the safe harbor amount is the same as April's. Ana pays about one thousand two hundred and ninety-six, Sam about three thousand and ten, and Jo about seven thousand one hundred and sixteen. If income dropped, the ninety percent method can lower the payment a lot, but recheck in the fall. Count any applied refund. Pay estimated tax for twenty twenty-seven, and check your state.
